slides.teaching: Tell students plainly: there is no new sklearn or scipy call today. Everything used in the demo has already run in Weeks 11, 13, or 14 — today is about the WIRING between them.

slides.title: Predict-optimize-decide, defined
slides.definition: The three-stage pattern this whole course builds toward: FIT and evaluate a model from data (predict), search using that fitted model as the objective or a constraint (optimize), then report the result next to the model's own uncertainty and limits (decide).

example.head: Where each word comes from
example.body: Predict = Weeks 13-14 (train_test_split, metrics, model card). Optimize = Weeks 10-12 (linprog, minimize, GA) applied to the fitted model instead of a hand-written formula. Decide = a bounded, uncertain recommendation, not a guarantee.

slides.note: This names how Weeks 9-14's tools already fit together — nothing new is taught in this sentence, only wired.
slides.teaching: Have students say the three words back with the week number each one came from before moving to the process diagram — this primes the whole session's arc.

slides.title: The predict-optimize-decide loop, recapped

steps.label: PREDICT
steps.head: Fit and evaluate a model
steps.body: Weeks 13-14: train_test_split, beat (or fail to beat) a naive baseline, report MAE/RMSE/R² or a confusion matrix, state a model card's scope and limits.

steps.label: OPTIMIZE
steps.head: Search using the fitted model
steps.body: Weeks 10-12's linprog/minimize/GA now takes the FITTED model as its objective or constraint — not a hand-written formula like Week 9/11's energy_proxy.

steps.label: DECIDE
steps.head: State a bounded recommendation
steps.body: Report the result next to the model's own uncertainty and training-range limits — an investigate-further finding, not a guarantee.

slides.teaching: Ask students to name, out loud, which week each of the three words came from, before moving on — this is the whole semester's arc in one slide.

slides.title: Recall: which fitted model feeds today's demo
slides.callout: Same predict-optimize-decide pattern either way — only whether the model becomes the objective or a constraint differs.

slides.title: Why this session looks different

Only the INTEGRATION: wiring a fitted model into minimize() as objective, or a classifier's prediction as constraint.

slides.title: Baseline design, defined
slides.definition: The fixed starting point for today's demo, held constant except where the optimizer is explicitly allowed to move it — the same role Week 11's starting guess played, now applied to a fitted model instead of a hand-written formula.

example.head: This session's baseline
example.body: wwr=0.50, shade_m=0.20, glazing_shgc=0.45, compactness=1.10, orientation=S. Only wwr and shade_m are handed to minimize() today — the SAME two variables and bounds as Weeks 9 and 11.

slides.note: orientation=S is a category, not a number fed to this 4-feature model at all — it stays part of the scenario's narrative, exactly as in Week 14, not a regression input.
slides.teaching: Point out orientation is a category (S), not a number fed to this 4-feature model at all — it is part of the scenario's narrative, not a regression input, exactly as in Week 14.

slides.title: Surrogate model, defined
slides.definition: A fitted model used as a fast stand-in for an expensive or unavailable simulation, so an optimizer can search against it directly instead of running the real simulation at every candidate design.

example.head: Today's surrogate
example.body: The Week 14 Track B 4-feature LinearRegression, refit here so the demo is self-contained — predicted EUI stands in for a full energy simulation at every (wwr, shade_m) the optimizer tries.

slides.note: Cross-validation measures performance stability across resamples; it is not an interval around an individual prediction. Use held-out residuals plus conformal/bootstrap methods when a prediction interval is needed.
slides.teaching: Refitting live (rather than loading a saved model file) is deliberate — students have not been taught model persistence, and re-running the exact fit keeps every number traceable to code on screen.

slides.title: Recall: Week 14's fitted 4-feature regressor
slides.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

portfolio = pd.read_csv('radley_portfolio_envelope.csv')
FEATURES = ['wwr','shade_m','glazing_shgc','compactness']
dev_idx, test_idx = train_test_split(
    np.arange(len(portfolio)), test_size=0.20, random_state=42)
surrogate = LinearRegression().fit(
    portfolio.loc[dev_idx, FEATURES],
    portfolio.loc[dev_idx, 'eui_kwh_m2yr'])
print('rows used for final fit:', len(dev_idx))
slides.explainHead: Use the already-selected specification; do not reopen model selection
slides.explainBody: Week 14 selected four features using training/validation and paired development folds. The final model is now refit on all 112 development rows. Final-test rows remain evaluation evidence, not optimization inputs.
slides.teaching: Point at random_state=42 and remind students it is the same value used for every split across Weeks 13-15, which is why the numbers on the next slide will match Week 14's exactly rather than merely closely.

slides.title: ...continued: confirm it is the same model
slides.code:
print(surrogate.coef_.round(4), round(surrogate.intercept_, 4))
print('Week 14 final test: MAE=1.9881 RMSE=2.5210 R2=0.5167')
slides.explainBody: These coefficients come from the final development-data refit. Their signs are associations, not causal effects, and final-test RMSE is not an individual prediction interval.
slides.teaching: Ask students to read the sign of each coefficient as a physical claim before moving on - all four match the direction Week 13 and Week 14 established, which is why this refit is a recall rather than a new result.

slides.title: Baseline predicted EUI
slides.code:
BASELINE = {'wwr': 0.50,
            'shade_m': 0.20,
            'glazing_shgc': 0.45,
            'compactness': 1.10}
row = np.array([[BASELINE['wwr'],
                 BASELINE['shade_m'],
                 BASELINE['glazing_shgc'],
                 BASELINE['compactness']]])
print(round(surrogate.predict(row)[0], 4))
slides.explainBody: 31.2886 kWh/m²/yr is the frozen final model's prediction for the baseline before optimization. The wrapper must reproduce it exactly to the reported precision.
slides.teaching: Write 31.2886 on the board and connect it to Week 14's hand-computed transfer check.

slides.title: Anatomy: the minimize() call that runs today's demo

parts.label: Optimizer
parts.body: The same scipy tool used in Week 11.

parts.label: Initial guess
parts.body: Starts from the baseline wwr and shade.

parts.label: Bounds
parts.body: Keeps both variables inside stated ranges.

slides.teaching: If a function maps decision variables to one predicted number, minimize can search it. All other features stay pinned at baseline.

slides.title: DEMO — the objective function itself
slides.code:
def surrogate_eui(design_vars: tuple) -> float:
    """Predicted EUI (kWh/m2/yr) at (wwr, shade_m)."""
    wwr, shade_m = design_vars
    row = np.array([[wwr, shade_m,
                     BASELINE['glazing_shgc'],
                     BASELINE['compactness']]])
    return surrogate.predict(row)[0]

print(round(surrogate_eui((0.50, 0.20)), 4))
slides.explainBody: Calling the wrapper at the baseline must reproduce 31.2886 before the optimizer is trusted. Use a DataFrame with the named feature columns to avoid silent column-order mistakes.
slides.teaching: This check-before-trusting habit is worth naming explicitly: always verify a wrapped objective function at a known point before handing it to an optimizer.

slides.title: Anatomy: unpacking surrogate.predict(row)[0]

parts.label: The fitted model object
parts.body: Week 14 Track B's regressor, already .fit() — not refit here.

parts.label: Predict needs a 2D row
parts.body: wwr, shade_m at the search point; shgc, compactness pinned at baseline.

parts.label: Pull the number back out
parts.body: .predict() always returns an array; [0] takes the lone value out.

slides.teaching: Both traps are genuine beginner errors worth naming explicitly: forgetting predict() needs a 2D row (not a flat list), and forgetting its return value is itself an array, not a bare number.

slides.title: DEMO 1 — minimize() from the baseline design
slides.code:
from scipy.optimize import minimize

bounds = [(0.20, 0.60), (0.0, 1.2)]
result = minimize(
    surrogate_eui, x0=(0.50, 0.20),
    bounds=bounds)
print('x:', result.x.round(4))
print('value:', round(result.fun, 4))
print('success:', result.success)
slides.explainHead: Both variables land exactly ON a bound
slides.explainBody: The linear surrogate pushes wwr to 0.20 and shade_m to 1.20. Predicted EUI falls from 31.2886 to 22.7503. This boundary candidate now requires a high-fidelity truth check.
slides.teaching: This is the reveal for the anatomy slide's minimize() call — walk result.x and result.fun against what that diagram named. A predict slide right before Demo 2 asks students to commit to an answer before it runs.

slides.title: Local optimum, recalled
slides.definition: A point where a search method gets stuck — better than every nearby point, but not necessarily the best point overall. Whether a fitted surrogate has one depends entirely on its own shape, not on the fact that it was fitted.

example.head: Week 11 vs. today
example.body: Week 11's energy_proxy had two basins: the local result near -7.08 and a lower best-known basin near -11.08, corroborated by a finite grid plus multistart rather than proved global. Five of eight starts reached the worse basin. Today's surrogate is affine in wwr and shade_m with other features fixed — no interior valley.

slides.note: This is a fact about THIS surrogate's linear shape, not a general claim about every fitted model.
slides.teaching: State the contrast in terms of this surrogate's shape, and keep Week 11's proof-versus-corroboration distinction precise.

slides.title: The surrogate's shape: no bends anywhere
slides.chartTitle: Predicted EUI across each variable's own bounds
slides.xTitle: position across the variable's own bounds
slides.explainHead: Two straight lines, not two basins
slides.explainBody: The final fitted coefficients are +17.7561 for wwr and −3.2115 for shade_m. Straight lines explain why different starts agree; they do not validate the surrogate.
slides.teaching: Both series computed by actually calling surrogate_eui at 5 evenly spaced points across each variable's full bound range, holding the other variable at baseline — verified, not sketched.

slides.title: Predict: does a different starting guess change the optimized design?
slides.code:
result2 = minimize(
    surrogate_eui, x0=(0.22, 1.10),
    bounds=bounds)
print('x:', result2.x.round(4))
print('value:', round(result2.fun, 4))
slides.question: Starting from x0=(0.22, 1.10) instead, where does minimize() land?
options: A different local optimum — Week 11's pattern repeats
The identical x=[0.20, 1.20], value=22.7503 — same as Demo 1
minimize() fails to converge from this far away
A different corner of the box, e.g. x=[0.60, 0.0]
slides.why: Both starts reach x=[0.20, 1.20], value=22.7503 because the fitted objective is linear in the two free variables. Agreement does not validate the surrogate.
slides.teaching: x0=(0.22, 1.10) is far from Demo 1's start and near Week 11's lower best-known basin on an unrelated problem. Have students commit before revealing; agreement is the finding here, not surrogate validation.

slides.title: DEMO 2 — only x0 changes
slides.code:
result2 = minimize(
    surrogate_eui, x0=(0.22, 1.10),
    bounds=bounds)
print('x:', result2.x.round(4))
print('value:', round(result2.fun, 4))
print('success:', result2.success)
slides.explainBody: This start is deliberately far from DEMO 1 and near Week 11's lower best-known basin on an unrelated problem. Both starts agree here; that says something about this affine objective, not about surrogate validity.
slides.teaching: Let the agreement land, then ask what it establishes and what it does not.

slides.title: Baseline vs. optimized, verified
slides.callout: Surrogate-predicted improvement: 8.5383 kWh/m²/yr (27.29%). Next: confirm the candidate with the non-surrogate simulator or measurement process.
slides.teaching: This is the exact table format Project 2 Part IV's baseline-vs-recommended figure should use — point that out explicitly.

slides.title: This bounded linear surrogate has no suboptimal local trap
slides.kicker: A precise claim about this model
slides.statement: On a bounded box, a linear objective has no suboptimal local trap: every local optimum is global, possibly along an optimal face.
slides.supporting: Different starts therefore agree here. Nonlinear models or nonconvex feasible sets can reintroduce suboptimal traps.
slides.teaching: Distinguish 'no suboptimal local optimum' from 'only one optimum.' A flat boundary face can contain multiple global optima.

slides.title: Constraint, recalled
slides.definition: A condition a candidate solution MUST satisfy, recalled from Week 10 — as opposed to the objective, which is the quantity being minimized or maximized. Today's Track A idea puts a fitted classifier's prediction on the constraint side instead of the objective side.

example.head: Track A's constraint, reused
example.body: predicted P(meets code) ≥ 0.5 — the Week 14 validation-selected policy. Treat it as a modeled screen, then verify feasibility with the real code/simulation check.

slides.note: A constraint does not get minimized — it only filters which candidate designs are allowed. Something ELSE (cost, EUI, or another objective) still gets minimized subject to it.
slides.teaching: Confirm students can state the difference between 'the quantity being minimized' and 'a condition that must hold' before the next slide applies it to Track A's classifier.

slides.title: Track A's constraint pattern, described
slides.kicker: Conceptual only — no separate numeric demo
rows: Track B (this demo): model IS the objective
minimize(surrogate_eui(...), x0=..., bounds=...) — the model's prediction is minimized.
Track A (conceptual): model becomes a CONSTRAINT
minimize(other_obj, ..., constraints=[P(meets code)≥0.5]) — a modeled screen, followed by truth-model verification.
slides.callout: Same predict-optimize-decide pattern either way — only whether the model becomes the objective or a constraint differs.
slides.teaching: Keep this conceptual, per the plan — no new numeric demo today. If a Track A student asks for the exact scipy.optimize.minimize constraints= syntax, offer to work through it one-on-one during the advising time later this session.

slides.title: Recall: which threshold did the validation rule select?
slides.kicker: Predict before you run — recall Week 14
slides.code:
# validation rule: FPR <= 10%, then maximize recall
# 0.4 fails; 0.5 and 0.6 qualify
# compare recall at the qualifying thresholds
slides.question: Which threshold was frozen before the final test?
slides.why: 0.5: validation FPR=5.3% and recall=0.667. Threshold 0.6 also meets the FPR limit but recall collapses to 0.111.
slides.teaching: Retrieve the frozen 0.5 policy and its validation rule before treating probability as a modeled constraint.

slides.title: State the recommendation as bounded and uncertain
slides.statement: The surrogate proposes wwr=0.20 and shade_m=1.20, with a predicted EUI reduction of about 8.54 kWh/m²/yr (27.29%), holding SHGC and compactness fixed.
slides.supporting: The candidate lies on two bounds and comes from a model with final-test RMSE=2.5210. RMSE is not a prediction interval. Run the high-fidelity simulator or measurement process at the baseline and candidate, then report both the surrogate error and the confirmed improvement.
slides.teaching: This sentence IS the predict-optimize-decide synthesis the whole session builds to. Have students read it aloud once before moving on.

slides.title: Recall: did the 4-feature gain recur across development folds?
slides.kicker: Predict before you run — recall Week 14
slides.code:
# paired folds on the 112 development rows
print('3-feature mean R2:', 0.2313)
print('4-feature mean R2:', 0.3225)
slides.question: What did paired development-fold evaluation support?
options: The 4-feature model on average, with variability
slides.why: Mean development-fold R² rises from 0.2313 to 0.3225. That supports the specification choice but is neither a causal result nor an individual interval.
slides.teaching: Use fold variation as model-stability evidence. The untouched final test is reported separately: MAE=1.9881, RMSE=2.5210, R²=0.5167.

slides.title: Predict: what happens at wwr=0.85?
slides.kicker: Predict before you run — recall Week 13
slides.code:
# Week 13's 3-feature model (wwr, shade_m, glazing_shgc)
row = np.array([[0.85, 0.60, 0.45]])
print(round(model_3feat.predict(row)[0], 4))
slides.question: wwr=0.85 is far outside the training range. What does the model return?
options: A ValueError, refusing to predict out of range
A visible warning, then a number
36.13 — a normal-looking number, no warning at all
slides.why: 36.13 -- a normal-looking number, no warning at all. Always check input ranges yourself; the model cannot warn you.
slides.teaching: wwr=0.85 exceeds Week 13's verified training range (0.201-0.592). The exact 3-feature model predicts 36.1307, which sits inside the observed EUI range (17.9-37.2) and therefore looks plausible. Ask how an explicit support gate would reveal the unsupported input.

slides.title: Two honesty checks, the numbers
rows: wwr=0.85 exceeds [0.201, 0.592], yet returns 36.13 without warning.
Validation R² 0.3903→0.4258; paired development-CV mean 0.2313→0.3225; final test once: MAE 1.9881, RMSE 2.5210, R² 0.5167.
slides.callout: Neither result is an individual prediction interval. Gate feature support, then confirm the optimized candidate in the non-surrogate truth model and report the discrepancy.
slides.teaching: Both checks belong directly in a Project 2 model card, not just in this deck.

slides.title: Five-minute capstone reviews leave time for synthesis

steps.label: DECISION
steps.head: 4 minutes — decision brief
steps.body: State variables, objective/constraint, baseline, recommended design, uncertainty, and one bounded recommendation sentence.

steps.label: TRACE
steps.head: 1 minute — evidence/code trace
steps.body: Show one evaluation artifact and the exact wrapper that calls the model as objective or constraint. Hard cap: 5 minutes total.

steps.label: SYNTHESIS
steps.head: 15 minutes — selective source-deck synthesis
steps.body: Reconnect the strongest evidence patterns across the semester. If enrollment exceeds 12, use parallel gallery/code-review rounds before reconvening.

slides.teaching: Enforce the 4+1 structure and five-minute hard cap. Reserve 15 minutes for selective source-deck synthesis; with more than 12 students, run parallel gallery/code-review rounds rather than serial talks.

slides.title: Reproducibility and AI-use-record, one more time
rows: random_state=42 on every split, a script that runs top to bottom after a kernel restart, and every reported number traceable to a printed cell output — the same standard as every prior week.
Project 2's deliverable list requires a filled-in AI-use record: tool/model, prompt, what you accepted/modified/rejected, and one limitation you found — not a blank template.

slides.title: A surrogate proposal graduates through independent verification

steps.label: SCREEN
steps.head: Surrogate
steps.body: Rank many supported candidates quickly and expose the model domain and uncertainty.

steps.label: SEARCH
steps.head: Optimizer
steps.body: Explore a bounded decision space with an explicit objective, constraints, budget, and seed.

steps.label: CONFIRM
steps.head: Truth model or measurement
steps.body: Re-run finalists in EnergyPlus, another domain simulator, measurement, or expert audit.

steps.label: BENCHMARK
steps.head: Repeatable test
steps.body: For controls, a framework such as BOPTEST supports comparable cases, KPIs, and baselines.

slides.teaching: EnergyPlus is one example of a higher-fidelity building simulation engine; BOPTEST is specifically a building-controls benchmarking framework, not a universal truth oracle. Require students to name the verification tool and discrepancy tolerance before accepting a recommendation.

slides.title: Risk management is a lifecycle—not a final disclaimer

left.head: Govern + map
left.body:
Name accountable people
Define intended use and refusal conditions
Map affected stakeholders and failure costs
Record data, model, solver, and AI provenance

right.head: Measure + manage
right.body:
Test validity, calibration, feasibility, and robustness
Monitor drift and subgroup performance
Escalate exceptions
Retire or revise when evidence no longer supports use

slides.teaching: Use the NIST AI RMF functions as a professional vocabulary. Students do not need to memorize the framework; they must show that technical evaluation and organizational responsibility continue after the demo works.

slides.title: The loop closes: predict, optimize, decide
takeaways: A fitted model can become an optimizer's objective or a modeled constraint.
One wrapper function connects .predict() or .predict_proba() to the search.
This linear surrogate has no local trap; that is a property of this model, not a general guarantee.
Report limits and calibrated intervals when available; confirm the candidate with the non-surrogate truth model.
slides.teaching: Close by reminding students that Project 2 is due only when the recommendation has a truth-model check and bounded claim.
